standard_text: Write an inequality of the form x > c, x ≥ c, x < c, or x ≤ c, where c is a rational number, to represent a constraint or condition in a real-world or other mathematical problem. Explain that inequalities have infinitely many solutions and how to represent solutions on a number line diagram.

skills.name: Compare whole numbers using the > and < symbols

prerequisite_skill.description: Compare two multi-digit whole numbers and record the comparison with >, <, or =.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: Write > or < to make this true: 358 __ 385

skills.i_do_script: The comparison symbol is a picture before it is a rule: its wide open side always sits next to the bigger amount, like a mouth facing the taller stack of blocks. Watch: to compare 358 and 385, I line up the places and compare from the left. Both have 3 hundreds, so I look at the tens: 5 tens against 8 tens. 385 has more, so the open side faces 385 and I write 358 < 385. I read it left to right: 358 is less than 385.

canonical_error.pattern: Reverses the meaning of < and >, or compares digits without attending to place
canonical_error.example: Writes 358 > 385, or says 47 > 74 because it starts with a bigger digit pair in their head
canonical_error.why: The student guesses the symbol from its shape instead of pointing the open side at the bigger number, or compares digits out of place order. Stacking base ten blocks makes the bigger pile, and the open side, obvious.

skills.item_template: Two whole numbers up to four digits. Student writes >, <, or = between them, or answers which is greater. Short response fluency bank, no context, no variables.

sample_items.answer: False

redirect_script.stop: Which number is actually bigger? Prove it with places.
redirect_script.prompt: Compare from the left, place by place: hundreds first, then tens, then ones. The wide open side of the symbol always faces the bigger number.
redirect_script.praise: You pointed the open side at the bigger number, that is exactly what the symbol means.

vocabulary.definition: The symbol > means the number on the left is bigger than the number on the right.
The symbol < means the number on the left is smaller than the number on the right.

next_steps.if_fail: Review grade 4 place value with base ten blocks: build both numbers and compare the piles before writing any symbol.

worked_example_script.text: Build 47 and 74 with base ten blocks: 4 rods and 7 cubes next to 7 rods and 4 cubes.
Which pile is bigger? How do the rods tell you before you even count the cubes?
74 has 7 tens against 4 tens, so 74 is bigger. The symbol's wide open side faces the bigger pile: 47 < 74. Read it left to right: 47 is less than 74.
If a student writes 47 > 74, have them point the open side at the bigger pile of blocks and re-read the sentence.
Your turn: write the symbol between 358 and 385, and read your sentence out loud.

skills.name: Plot whole numbers and fractions on a number line

prerequisite_skill.description: Locate a whole number or a fraction like 3/4 or 5/4 on a number line with labeled whole number ticks.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: Between which two whole numbers does 5/4 sit on a number line?

skills.i_do_script: A number line is a walking path: I start at 0 and every step to the right makes the number bigger. Watch: to plot 3/4, I cut the space between 0 and 1 into 4 equal steps and walk 3 of them. I land between 0 and 1, closer to 1. To plot 5/4, I walk 4 fourths to reach 1, then 1 more fourth, so 5/4 lands between 1 and 2. The bottom number tells the step size, the top number counts the steps.

canonical_error.pattern: Plots a fraction at the whole number matching its numerator or denominator
canonical_error.example: Plots 3/4 at 3, or plots 5/4 between 4 and 5 because of the 4
canonical_error.why: The student reads the fraction's digits as locations instead of as a count of equal steps. Walking the steps on a drawn line shows 3/4 never leaves the space between 0 and 1.

skills.item_template: One whole number or positive fraction (denominators 2, 3, 4, 6, 8). Student names where it sits: between which whole numbers, closer to which end, or which tick shows it. Short response fluency bank.

sample_items.stem: Between which two whole numbers is 5/4?
sample_items.answer: 1 and 2

sample_items.stem: A line from 0 to 1 is cut into 4 equal parts. Which fraction is at the second tick after 0?
Between which two whole numbers is 7/2?
sample_items.answer: 3 and 4

sample_items.stem: Which is farther right on a number line: 2 or 5?
What number is at the halfway mark between 2 and 3?
Between which two whole numbers is 8/3?
sample_items.answer: 2 and 3

redirect_script.stop: What size is one step, and how many steps do you walk?
redirect_script.prompt: Start at 0. The bottom number cuts each whole into equal steps, the top number counts the steps you walk to the right.
redirect_script.praise: You walked the steps instead of jumping to the digit, that is how a number line works.

vocabulary.definition: A line that shows numbers in order, getting bigger as you move right.
A small mark on a number line that shows exactly where a number sits.

next_steps.if_fail: Review grade 3 fractions on a number line with a folded paper strip: fold a 0 to 1 strip into fourths and walk 3/4 with a finger.

worked_example_script.text: Draw a number line from 0 to 2 and cut each whole into 4 equal steps.
To plot 5/4, what size is one step, and how many do we walk from 0?
Each step is one fourth. Walk 4 steps to land exactly on 1, then 1 more step. 5/4 sits between 1 and 2, one fourth past 1.
If a student heads toward 5 or toward 4, stop them at 1: how many fourths did it take to get here? How many are left?
Your turn: plot 3/4 on this line. Between which whole numbers does it land?

skills.name: Compare two decimals to the hundredths

prerequisite_skill.description: Compare two decimals to the hundredths using place value and record the comparison with >, <, or =.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: Which is greater, 0.5 or 0.35? How do you know?

skills.i_do_script: Every digit in a decimal has a place, and the place tells its size. Watch: to compare 0.5 and 0.35, I compare the tenths first: 5 tenths against 3 tenths. Five tenths is more, so 0.5 > 0.35 even though 35 looks bigger than 5. On a hundredths grid, 0.5 shades 50 squares and 0.35 shades only 35. More digits does not mean a bigger number, the places decide.

canonical_error.pattern: Compares decimals like whole numbers, ignoring place value
canonical_error.why: The student strips the decimal point and compares the leftover digits as whole numbers. The hundredths grid shows 0.5 covers more squares, so longer does not mean larger.

skills.item_template: Two decimals to the hundredths. Student writes >, <, or = between them or names which is greater. Short response fluency bank, no context, no negatives.

sample_items.answer: False

redirect_script.stop: Which place are you comparing first?
redirect_script.prompt: Line up the decimal points and compare place by place, starting with the largest place. Tenths beat hundredths no matter how many digits follow.
redirect_script.praise: You compared the tenths first, that is exactly how place value works.

vocabulary.definition: The first place to the right of the decimal point; one tenth is 1/10 or 0.1.
The second place to the right of the decimal point; one hundredth is 1/100 or 0.01.

next_steps.if_fail: Review grade 4 decimal notation with a hundredths grid: shade each decimal and compare the shaded areas before writing any symbol.

worked_example_script.text: Shade 0.5 on one hundredths grid and 0.35 on another.
Which grid has more shading? So which number is greater?
0.5 shades 50 of the 100 squares and 0.35 shades 35. So 0.5 > 0.35. The tenths digit decides it: 5 tenths beats 3 tenths.
If a student says 0.35 is greater because 35 > 5, send them back to the grids: which covers more?
Your turn: which is greater, 0.6 or 0.58?

skills.name: Compare and order decimals to the thousandths

prerequisite_skill.description: Compare two decimals to the thousandths using place value, and order a set of three decimals.

skills.i_do_script: Comparing decimals is a place by place contest, starting from the biggest place. Watch: to compare 0.406 and 0.46, I line up the decimal points and pad with a zero so both show thousandths: 0.406 against 0.460. Tenths tie at 4. Hundredths: 0 against 6, and 6 wins, so 0.46 is greater. I never count digits, I compare places. On a place value chart the contest is over the moment one place wins.

canonical_error.pattern: Treats more decimal digits as a bigger number
canonical_error.why: The student strips the point and compares whole numbers. Padding both decimals to the same length, 0.406 against 0.460, makes the place by place contest honest and shows 460 thousandths is more.

skills.item_template: Two or three positive decimals to the thousandths. Student writes >, <, or = or orders the set from least to greatest. Numeric or short response, no calculator, no negatives.

sample_items.distractor_logic: Digit counters pick 0.406 because 406 > 46.
Students who ignore the middle zero call them equal or flip the symbol.
Digit counters pick 0.699 because it is longer.
Digit counters put 0.303 first because it looks longest.
Students who count digits say 0.250 is greater.
Students comparing 09 to 1 as whole numbers say 1.1 is less.
Digit counters pick 3.68 because 68 > 7.
Padding to 0.500, 0.502, 0.520 settles it; digit counters scramble the middle.

redirect_script.stop: Are you comparing places or counting digits?
redirect_script.prompt: Line up the decimal points and pad with zeros until both numbers are the same length. Then compare place by place from the left, and stop at the first place that differs.
redirect_script.praise: You padded and compared place by place, so the longer number could not fool you.

vocabulary.definition: The third place to the right of the decimal point; one thousandth is 1/1000 or 0.001.
Decimals that name the same amount, like 0.25 and 0.250; trailing zeros do not change the value.

worked_example_script.text: Write 0.406 and 0.46 stacked with the decimal points lined up, then pad: 0.406 over 0.460.
Why can I write 0.46 as 0.460 without changing it?
A trailing zero adds no value: 46 hundredths is 460 thousandths. Now compare places from the left: tenths tie 4 to 4, hundredths 0 against 6, so 0.460 wins. 0.46 > 0.406.
If a student says 0.406 is greater because 406 > 46, point at the padded pair: which has more thousandths, 406 or 460?
Your turn: pad and compare 0.7 and 0.699.

practice_problems.stem: Which is greater: 0.6 or 0.42?
True or false: 0.30 = 0.3
practice_problems.answer: True

practice_problems.stem: Order least to greatest: 1.02, 1.2, 1.22
Name a decimal that sits between 0.4 and 0.41.
practice_problems.answer: Any decimal like 0.405 (0.401 through 0.409 all work)

practice_problems.stem: Maya wrote 0.35 > 0.5 because 35 is bigger than 5. Find her mistake and fix it.
practice_problems.answer: She stripped the decimal points and compared whole numbers. Pad to 0.35 and 0.50: 50 hundredths beats 35 hundredths, so 0.5 > 0.35.

activities.title: Grid the Contest
activities.instructions:
1. Each pair draws two decimal cards, like 0.46 and 0.406.
2. Shade each on its own hundredths grid, treating a thousandths digit as part of one square.
3. Compare the shaded areas and write the true symbol sentence, like 0.46 > 0.406.
4. Then check the picture with the pad and compare routine: line up points, pad zeros, compare places.
5. Repeat with 0.7 and 0.699. Say each time: places decide, not digit counts.

activities.title: Order Up
materials: Deck of decimal cards (tenths, hundredths, thousandths mixed)
activities.instructions:
1. Deal each player three decimal cards.
2. On go, each player lays their cards in order from least to greatest.
3. The group checks each lineup by padding every card to thousandths out loud.
4. One point per correct lineup; the padding reader catches any digit counting slip.
5. Shuffle and redeal; first to three points wins.

strategy_links.why: Shading hundredths grids makes 'longer is not larger' visible before the pad and compare routine is named.
The digit counting error is stable and predictable; finding and fixing it in shown work confronts it directly.

questioning_prompts: Which place did you compare first, and why that one?
Why does padding 0.46 to 0.460 not change its value?
Where did the contest end, which place broke the tie?
Show me on the grid: which number covers more?
Give me a decimal between these two. How do you know it fits?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student says the decimal with more digits is greater.
misconception_redirects.say: Pad both numbers to the same length and read them as thousandths. Which count is bigger, 406 or 460?
misconception_redirects.praise: You compared equal length names, so the extra digits could not trick you.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student lines up the digits from the right instead of lining up the decimal points.
misconception_redirects.say: Decimal points anchor the places. Stack the points in one column first, then every digit sits over its own place.
misconception_redirects.praise: You anchored the points, so tenths compared to tenths.

quick_checks.look_for: 0.7, with padding to 0.700 or a place value argument, not a digit count.
= with the trailing zero named as valueless.

steps.math: line up: 0.406 over 0.46
steps.annotation: Stack the decimal points so each place sits over its match.
A trailing zero adds no value; now both show thousandths.

steps.math: tenths: 4 = 4; hundredths: 0 < 6
steps.annotation: Compare from the left; the first place that differs decides.
460 thousandths is more than 406 thousandths.

steps.math: line up: 0.52 over 0.502
steps.annotation: Stack the decimal points in one column.
Pad with a zero so both show thousandths.
Compare place by place from the left. Which place breaks the tie?
Write the true symbol sentence.

The ___ place broke the tie because ___ is more than ___.

skills.name: Plot fractions, mixed numbers, and decimals on a number line

prerequisite_skill.description: Locate a positive fraction, mixed number, or decimal on a number line, naming which whole numbers it sits between.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: Between which two whole numbers does 7/4 sit on a number line?

skills.i_do_script: Any positive fraction or decimal has exactly one home on the number line, and renaming finds it. Watch: to plot 7/4, I rename it as a mixed number: 7/4 is 4/4 plus 3/4, which is 1 3/4. So it sits between 1 and 2, three fourths of the way along, closer to 2. To plot 2.3, I go to 2, then 3 tenths of the way toward 3. Rename first, then walk: whole number part first, fraction part after.

canonical_error.pattern: Places a fraction near the whole number in its numerator or denominator
canonical_error.example: Plots 7/4 between 7 and 8 because of the 7, or at 4 because of the 4
canonical_error.why: The student reads the fraction's digits as an address instead of renaming it. Converting to the mixed number 1 3/4 first forces the whole number part to pick the neighborhood before the fraction part fine tunes the spot.

skills.item_template: One positive fraction, mixed number, or decimal (denominators up to 8, decimals to hundredths). Student names which whole numbers it sits between, which of two values is farther right, or which tick shows it. Short response, no negatives.

sample_items.stem: Between which two whole numbers is 7/4?
sample_items.answer: 1 and 2
sample_items.distractor_logic: Digit readers say 7 and 8 or 4 and 5.

sample_items.stem: Between which two whole numbers is 2.3?
sample_items.answer: 2 and 3
sample_items.distractor_logic: Students who read 2.3 as 23 lose the neighborhood.
Students may say 5 1/2 or 2 1/5.

sample_items.stem: Which is farther right on a number line: 1.8 or 1.75?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Digit counters pick 1.75 because 75 > 8.
Students who see the 8 may reach for 1.

sample_items.stem: What number is halfway between 3 and 4?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Baseline check that halves anchor the walk.

sample_items.stem: Between which two whole numbers is 13/4?
sample_items.answer: 3 and 4
sample_items.distractor_logic: Digit readers say 13 and 14 or 4 and 5.

sample_items.answer: Yes
sample_items.distractor_logic: Students who read 09 as 9 tenths may misplace it past 2.5 but still inside; digit strippers may say no.

redirect_script.stop: Rename it first: what is the whole number part?
redirect_script.prompt: Turn the fraction into a mixed number, or read the decimal's whole number part. The whole number picks which two ticks it lives between, the leftover fraction walks you inside.
redirect_script.praise: You renamed before you plotted, so the digits could not send you to the wrong neighborhood.

vocabulary.definition: A whole number and a fraction together, like 1 3/4, naming the same amount as an improper fraction like 7/4.
A friendly anchor on the number line, like 0, 1/2, or 1, used to judge where a number sits.

worked_example_script.text: Draw a number line from 0 to 3 with fourths ticked between the whole numbers.
We want to plot 7/4. How many fourths make one whole? So how many wholes are inside 7/4?
Four fourths make 1, so 7/4 is 1 whole and 3 fourths more: 1 3/4. Start at 1, walk 3 fourths toward 2, and mark the spot. It lands between 1 and 2, closer to 2.
If a student heads toward 7, stop them: rename 7/4 as a mixed number first. What is the whole number part?
Your turn: rename 5/2 and plot it. Between which whole numbers does it land?

practice_problems.stem: Between which two whole numbers is 3/2?
practice_problems.answer: 1 and 2

practice_problems.stem: Where does 0.5 sit on a line from 0 to 1?
practice_problems.answer: Exactly halfway between 0 and 1

practice_problems.stem: Between which two whole numbers is 9/4?
practice_problems.answer: 2 and 3

practice_problems.stem: Which is farther right on a number line: 2.09 or 2.9?
Write 13/4 as a mixed number and name the whole numbers it sits between.
practice_problems.answer: 3 1/4, between 3 and 4

practice_problems.stem: Is 1.75 closer to 1 or to 2?
A line from 0 to 1 is cut into eighths. Which tick after 0 shows 5/8, and is it left or right of 1/2?
practice_problems.answer: The 5th tick; right of 1/2 because 5/8 > 4/8

practice_problems.stem: Leo plotted 7/4 between 7 and 8. Find his mistake and fix it.
shown_work: The 7 is the big number, so it goes near 7
practice_problems.answer: He read the numerator as an address. Rename: 7/4 = 1 3/4, so it sits between 1 and 2, three fourths past 1.

activities.title: Clothesline Numbers
materials: String stretched across the desk as a number line
activities.instructions:
1. Pin 0, 1, 2, and 3 on the string, evenly spaced.
2. Students take turns drawing a number card, renaming it out loud (7/4 is 1 3/4), and pinning it on the string.
3. The group checks each placement: right neighborhood first, then position inside.
4. When all cards hang, read the line left to right to confirm the order makes sense.
5. Say each time: whole number picks the neighborhood, fraction walks inside.

activities.title: Name the Neighborhood
materials: Card deck: one card per number, one card per neighborhood description
activities.instructions:
1. Spread the neighborhood cards face up.
2. Partner A flips a number card and renames it before touching anything.
3. Partner B finds the matching neighborhood card; both must agree.

strategy_links.why: The clothesline makes renaming physical: the whole number part visibly picks the neighborhood before any symbol work.
The numerator as address error is the canonical miss; fixing Leo's plot confronts it head on.
Renaming out loud before pinning makes the invisible first step audible and checkable.

What did you rename it as before you plotted?
Which two whole numbers is it between, and which is it closer to?
Is it left or right of 1/2? How do you know?
Show me with your finger: where does the walk start and where does it end?

misconception_redirects.say: The digits are not an address. Rename it as a mixed number first: the whole number part picks the neighborhood.
misconception_redirects.praise: You renamed first, so the plot landed in the right neighborhood.

misconception_redirects.praise: You read the places, so the walk lengths came out right.

1.8, with a tenths argument, not a digit count.

Start at the whole number and walk the leftover fraction.

skills.name: Match a written inequality to the number line that represents its solutions

prerequisite_skill.description: Given an inequality like x < -7/4, identify the correct number-line graph (open vs. closed circle, arrow direction).
prerequisite_skill.check_question: Which graph shows x ≥ 3: closed circle at 3 with arrow right, or open circle at 3 with arrow left?

skills.i_do_script: A number-line graph is a record of test results: every number that makes x < -7/4 true gets covered, and every number that fails the test -- including the boundary itself -- gets left out. When I match an inequality to a number line, I check two things. One: the circle. If the symbol is < or > (no line under it), the circle is OPEN because that boundary value is NOT a solution. If the symbol is ≤ or ≥, the circle is CLOSED (filled in) because the boundary IS a solution. Two: the arrow direction. If the symbol points to less than (< or ≤), the arrow goes LEFT. If it's greater than (> or ≥), the arrow goes RIGHT. For x < -7/4, the symbol is strict <, so OPEN circle at -7/4, arrow LEFT.

canonical_error.pattern: Student uses the wrong circle type (open vs. closed) by ignoring whether the equal sign is included in the symbol.
canonical_error.example: For x ≤ 5, student picks an open circle at 5 instead of a closed circle, because they only paid attention to the < part of ≤.
canonical_error.why: Student treats ≤ the same as <, missing that the bar under the symbol means 'include the boundary.' This is the same kind of miss as confusing 'at most' with 'less than.'

redirect_script.stop: Pause — check the symbol again, all of it.
redirect_script.prompt: First run the boundary number itself through the inequality -- does it pass the test or fail it? Look at the inequality. Is there a line UNDER the < or > symbol? If yes, the circle is closed (filled). If no, the circle is open (hollow). Then check direction: less-than arrows go LEFT, greater-than arrows go RIGHT.
redirect_script.praise: You read the whole symbol and got both the circle and the direction right.

vocabulary.definition: All the values that make an inequality true — there are infinitely many.
An unfilled circle on a number line that means the boundary value is NOT a solution (used for < and >).
A filled circle on a number line that means the boundary value IS a solution (used for ≤ and ≥).

next_steps.if_pass: Move to 6AF4-S2: write an inequality from a real-world constraint.
next_steps.if_fail: Re-teach 6AF4-F1 (symbol direction) and 6AF4-F3 (plotting boundary). Practice matching with a small set of inequalities and four graph options each.

skills.item_template: A written inequality with a rational boundary (fraction, decimal, or negative). Student picks the number-line graph from 4 described choices (circle type + arrow direction). MC.

worked_example_script.text: Before we draw anything, run two numbers through the test x < -7/4. Is -3 less than -7/4? (Yes -- -3 sits farther left.) Now the boundary itself: is -7/4 less than -7/4? (No -- a number can't be less than itself.)

So the graph must cover -3 but leave -7/4 itself out -- that's why the circle at the boundary stays hollow, and the shading runs left where the passing numbers live. The picture is just the record of who passed.
Write x < -7/4 on the board and sketch a number line from -3 to 1 with tick marks at every whole number.
Before we touch the graph: where does -7/4 live on this line? Say it as a mixed number first.
If the student places -7/4 to the right of zero or right of -1, pause and have them count LEFT from zero: down one whole to -1, then three fourths more toward -2.
Now the circle. Does the symbol < have a bar under it? So is -7/4 itself a solution?
Open or closed circle, then?
Read the inequality with the variable first: 'x is less than -7/4.' Do the solutions live to the left or the right of the circle?
Draw the open circle at -7/4 and the arrow pointing left. Test it: mark -3 (a solution, the arrow covers it) and 0 (not a solution, the arrow misses it).
Same two decisions as always -- circle from the bar, direction from reading variable-first. The fraction only changes WHERE the circle goes, not how you decide.

practice_problems.stem: Between which two integers does -3/2 sit on a number line?
practice_problems.answer: Between -2 and -1

practice_problems.stem: For x <= 1.5, is 1.5 itself a solution?
practice_problems.answer: Yes -- the bar under <= means the boundary is included.

practice_problems.stem: Graph the solutions of x > -2.5 on the number line.
practice_problems.answer: Open circle at -2.5, arrow pointing right
practice_problems.notes: Two traps: placing -2.5 on the wrong side of -2, and closing the circle.

practice_problems.stem: Which number line represents n <= -7/4: a closed circle at -7/4 with the arrow left, or an open circle at -7/4 with the arrow left?
practice_problems.answer: Closed circle at -7/4, arrow left -- the bar under <= means -7/4 itself is a solution.

practice_problems.stem: Ava matched the inequality x >= -0.5 to a graph. Find her mistake and fix it.
shown_work: Ava's choice: open circle at -0.5, arrow pointing right
practice_problems.answer: The arrow is right, but the circle must be CLOSED. Ava treated >= like > and ignored the bar -- the boundary -0.5 IS a solution, so the circle is filled in.
practice_problems.notes: Canonical error: dropping the 'or equal to' part of the symbol.

practice_problems.stem: Graph the solutions of t < 3/4 on the number line.
practice_problems.answer: Open circle at 3/4, arrow pointing left
practice_problems.notes: Boundary between 0 and 1; open circle because < has no bar.

practice_problems.stem: A graph shows a closed circle at -1.25 with the arrow pointing left. Write the inequality it represents.
practice_problems.notes: Reversed direction: from graph back to symbols.

practice_problems.stem: How many solutions does x > 2.5 have? Explain how the graph shows your answer.
practice_problems.answer: Infinitely many. The arrow never ends -- every number greater than 2.5 (like 2.6, 3, 100) is a solution, and there is no biggest one.

activities.title: Inequality-Graph Match-Up
materials: Graph-description cards (or mini sketched number lines)
activities.instructions:
1. Spread the graph cards face up. Stack the inequality cards face down.
2. Partner A flips an inequality and says the two decisions out loud: 'bar or no bar' and 'variable-first, which direction.'
3. Partner B finds the matching graph. Both must agree before the pair is set aside.
4. Two decoy graphs never get matched -- when only decoys remain, partners explain what inequality each decoy WOULD represent.
5. Debrief question: which pair was hardest, and which of the two decisions made it hard?

activities.title: The Missing Bar
materials: One printed problem card per group
activities.instructions:
1. Show the group Ava's match for x >= -0.5 and let them react first.
2. Ask: what was Ava thinking? (Her arrow logic was perfect -- she only missed one thing.)
3. Have the group state the rule that separates > from >= in their own words.
4. Each student writes one sentence: how do you check a circle before you commit?

content.worked_problem: Inequality: x >= -0.5. Ava's choice: open circle at -0.5, arrow pointing right.
content.error_step: Ava read >= as plain > and drew an open circle at the boundary.
content.why: The bar under >= means -0.5 itself makes the inequality true, so the circle must be filled in. Open circles are only for < and >, where the boundary is left out.

strategy_links.why: Words to symbol to number-line picture is a representation chain -- CRA makes students move deliberately between the symbolic and the visual.
The open-vs-closed miss is a precise, findable bug -- analyzing a wrong match surfaces it faster than more correct examples.
Whiteboard Pass lets you see every student's circle and arrow on the same inequality in one glance.

questioning_prompts: Before anything else: where does that boundary number live? Say it as a mixed number if it helps.
Does the symbol have a bar under it? What does the bar buy you?
Read it variable-first for me. Which side of the circle do the solutions live on?
Name one number the arrow covers and prove it makes the inequality true.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student uses the wrong circle type (open vs. closed) by ignoring whether the equal sign is included in the symbol.
misconception_redirects.say: Look at the inequality. Is there a line UNDER the < or > symbol? If yes, the circle is closed (filled). If no, the circle is open (hollow). Then check direction: less-than arrows go LEFT, greater-than arrows go RIGHT.
misconception_redirects.praise: You read the whole symbol and got both the circle and the direction right.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student places a negative boundary like -7/4 on the positive side of zero, or between the wrong pair of integers.
misconception_redirects.say: Find zero first. The number is negative, so count to the LEFT: one whole to -1, then keep going. Which two integers does it land between?
misconception_redirects.praise: You located the boundary first -- now the circle and arrow have somewhere to live.

quick_checks.prompt: Point on a number line: where does -7/4 go?
quick_checks.look_for: A point between -2 and -1, closer to -2. A point on the positive side signals a sign-blindness gap (send back to 6AF4-F3), not an inequality problem.

quick_checks.prompt: Thumbs up or down: the graph of x <= -1.5 has a closed circle.
quick_checks.look_for: Instant thumbs-up. A thumbs-down means the student is still reading <= as < -- the exact canonical error.

worked_solution.answer: Open circle at -7/4, arrow pointing left

steps.math: -7/4 = -1 3/4, so the boundary sits between -2 and -1
steps.annotation: Locate the boundary first. Negative means count LEFT from zero: one whole, then three fourths more.

steps.math: Symbol check: < has NO bar, so the circle is OPEN
steps.annotation: No bar means -7/4 itself is not a solution -- the circle stays hollow.

steps.math: Read variable-first: 'x is less than -7/4' -> arrow LEFT
steps.annotation: Solutions are smaller than the boundary, and smaller numbers live to the left.

steps.math: Open circle at -7/4, arrow pointing left
steps.annotation: Check it: -3 is under the arrow and -3 < -7/4 is true. 0 is not, and 0 < -7/4 is false.

faded_example.answer: Closed circle at -0.5, arrow pointing right

steps.math: Locate the boundary: -0.5 is half a unit to the LEFT of zero
steps.annotation: Negative means left of zero -- halfway to -1.
Symbol check: does >= have a bar under it? So is the circle open or closed?
Read it variable-first and finish the graph: which way does the arrow point, and why?

sentence_starters: I placed the circle at ___ because the boundary is between ___ and ___.
The circle is ___ because the symbol ___ include the boundary.

skills.name: Write an inequality from a real-world constraint with one rational boundary

prerequisite_skill.description: Translate a single real-world constraint (with whole numbers, integers, or decimals) into an inequality of the form x > c, x ≥ c, x < c, or x ≤ c.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: A freezer must stay below -18 degrees. Write an inequality for t, the freezer's temperature.

skills.i_do_script: To write an inequality from a story, I do three steps. One: pick the variable — the problem usually names it (like t for temperature, g for gigabytes). Two: find the boundary number in the problem. Three: pick the symbol from the keyword. Watch: 'A freezer must stay below -18 degrees.' Variable: t. Boundary: -18. Keyword: 'below' → strict less than → t < -18. The boundary -18 itself is NOT allowed because 'below' doesn't include the boundary.

canonical_error.pattern: Student writes the inequality with the variable and boundary swapped or with the wrong direction symbol because they wrote it in the order of the words rather than checking which value is bigger.
canonical_error.example: For 'A balance must stay above 25 dollars,' student writes 25 > b instead of b > 25, treating the words as a literal left-to-right transcription.
canonical_error.why: Student is mapping word order to symbol position rather than asking 'which side is bigger?' They have not yet internalized that the inequality must hold true regardless of which side the variable is on.

redirect_script.stop: Wait — check which value is supposed to be bigger.
redirect_script.prompt: Read your inequality out loud. Does it match the story? If the story says the balance must stay ABOVE 25, then the balance b must be the bigger value. The wide side of the symbol must face b.
redirect_script.praise: You made the symbol point the right way — the variable side is the bigger side.

vocabulary.definition: A letter that stands for an unknown value in a math statement.
A rule from the problem that limits which values the variable can take.
A math statement that uses <, >, ≤, or ≥ to compare a variable with a number.

next_steps.if_pass: Move to 6AF4-S3: write the inequality AND graph the solutions on a number line.
next_steps.if_fail: Re-teach 6AF4-F2 (keyword to symbol). Practice with three short stories where the student underlines the keyword, the boundary, and writes the inequality step by step.

skills.item_template: A one-constraint real-world situation (whole numbers, integers, or decimals) naming a variable. Student writes the inequality. EQ response (type the inequality).

worked_example_script.text: Write the problem: 'A freezer must stay below -18 degrees Celsius. Write an inequality for t, the freezer's temperature.'
First job: what letter is our variable, and what does it stand for in this story?
Second job: what's the boundary number -- the number the story compares everything to?
Third job: the keyword. Underline the word that compares t to -18. Can the temperature EQUAL -18 and still count as 'below' it?
So which symbol: <, <=, >, or >=?
Write t < -18. Read it out loud together: 't is less than negative 18.'
Now check it with a real number. Is -20 below -18? Plug it in: does -20 make t < -18 true?

If the student writes t > -18 or -18 < t with the wrong meaning, don't correct -- have them test -20: 'The freezer is at -20 degrees. Is the food frozen? Does YOUR inequality say -20 works?' Let the test expose the flip.

practice_problems.stem: 'Riders must be at least 48 inches tall.' Which symbol will the inequality use?
practice_problems.answer: >= (at least means the boundary is included)

practice_problems.stem: 'The bus can hold no more than 40 students.' Which symbol will the inequality use?
practice_problems.answer: <= (no more than means 40 itself is still allowed)

practice_problems.stem: A package must weigh less than 20 pounds to ship free. Write an inequality for w, the weight in pounds.
A bank account balance must stay above -5 dollars to avoid a fee. Write an inequality for b, the balance in dollars.
practice_problems.notes: Negative boundary. Watch for b < -5 from students who hear 'avoid a fee' as a limit going down.

practice_problems.stem: Dev wrote an inequality for b, the balance in dollars. Find his mistake and fix it.
shown_work: Problem: The balance must stay above 25 dollars.
practice_problems.answer: Dev copied the word order: '25' then 'above-ish symbol' then 'b.' But 25 > b says the balance is BELOW 25 -- the opposite of the story. 'Above 25' means b is the bigger value: b > 25.
practice_problems.notes: Canonical error: transcribing word order instead of asking which value is bigger.

practice_problems.stem: Players must be at least 13 years old to join the league. Write an inequality for a, a player's age.
practice_problems.notes: Watch for a > 13 -- dropping the equal sign locks a 13-year-old out.

practice_problems.stem: Write a real-world sentence that the inequality g <= 3.5 could represent.
practice_problems.answer: Any sensible constraint, e.g. 'You may use up to 3.5 gigabytes of free data each month.'
practice_problems.notes: Producing the story shows the mapping runs both directions.

practice_problems.stem: The wind chill must be at least -10 degrees for outdoor recess. Write the inequality for w, then name one temperature that allows recess and one that does not.
practice_problems.answer: w >= -10. Works: 0 (0 >= -10 is true). Does not: -15 (-15 >= -10 is false).
practice_problems.notes: Negatives flip intuition -- students often claim -15 is 'more' than -10 because 15 > 10.

activities.title: Keyword-to-Symbol Sort
activities.instructions:
1. Lay the four symbol headers across the desk.
2. Partners take turns drawing a phrase card, reading it aloud, and placing it under a symbol.
3. Before placing, the drawer must answer one question out loud: 'Can the value EQUAL the number, or not?' If yes, the symbol needs the bar.
4. The partner agrees or challenges; a challenge means both explain, then check.
5. Debrief question: which phrases include the boundary, and what word tips you off?

activities.title: Why Did Dev Flip It?
materials: One printed problem card per group
activities.instructions:
1. Show the group Dev's inequality 25 > b and let them talk first.
2. Ask: what was Dev thinking? (He wrote the numbers and symbol in the same order he read them -- a sensible-sounding move.)
3. Have the group test a balance of 30 dollars: is it above 25? Does 25 > 30 come out true?
4. Each student writes Dev a one-sentence tip about checking which side is BIGGER.

content.worked_problem: Problem: 'The balance must stay above 25 dollars.' Dev wrote: 25 > b.
content.error_step: Dev transcribed the sentence left to right instead of asking which value must be bigger.
content.why: 'Above 25' makes the balance b the bigger value, so the wide-open side of the symbol must face b: b > 25. Dev's version says the balance is below 25 -- the exact opposite of the story.

activities.title: Constraint Showdown
activities.instructions:
1. Read a constraint aloud: 'A ride requires riders to be at least 42 inches tall. The variable is h.'
2. On 'show,' every student writes the full inequality and holds it up at once.
3. Pick one student with the majority answer and one with a different answer to each defend their symbol choice in one sentence.
4. Settle it with a test number: 'A rider is exactly 42 inches. Can they ride? Does your inequality agree?'
5. Keep a 'trap phrase' list of any constraint that split the room.

strategy_links.why: Partners debating 'does the boundary count?' before committing forces the at-least-vs-more-than distinction into words.
Gradual release fits the three-step routine (variable, boundary, keyword) -- model it, share it, then let students run it alone.
Analyzing a flipped inequality like 25 > b teaches the test-a-value habit that catches direction errors.

questioning_prompts: What does the variable stand for in this story -- the thing that can change, or the limit?
Underline the keyword. Can the value EQUAL the boundary and still follow the rule?
Read your inequality out loud. Does the sentence you just said match the story?
Give me a number that should work in the story. Does it make your inequality true?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student writes the inequality with the variable and boundary swapped or the wrong direction symbol because they wrote it in the order of the words rather than checking which value is bigger.
misconception_redirects.say: Read your inequality out loud. Does it match the story? If the story says the balance must stay ABOVE 25, then the balance b must be the bigger value. The wide side of the symbol must face b.
misconception_redirects.praise: You made the symbol point the right way -- the variable side is the bigger side.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student writes a strict inequality (< or >) for 'at least' or 'no more than,' dropping the boundary value.
misconception_redirects.say: Ask the boundary question: can the value BE exactly that number and still follow the rule? If a rider is exactly 48 inches, do they ride? If yes, your symbol needs the bar under it.
misconception_redirects.praise: You caught the boundary -- that's the difference between > and >=.

quick_checks.prompt: In one breath: 'Tickets cost under 12 dollars. Variable p.' Write the inequality.
quick_checks.look_for: p < 12 fast. A p > 12 signals direction flipping; p <= 12 signals the student adds the bar by default without asking the boundary question.

quick_checks.prompt: You wrote a >= 13 for 'at least 13 years old.' Is a 13-year-old allowed in? How does your symbol say so?
quick_checks.look_for: A confident 'yes -- the bar under >= includes 13.' Hesitation means the symbol was pattern-matched from the keyword chart, not understood.

worked_solution.stem: A freezer must stay below -18 degrees Celsius. Write an inequality for t, the freezer's temperature.

steps.math: Variable: t = the freezer's temperature. Boundary: -18
steps.annotation: Name the letter and find the number the story compares everything to.

steps.math: Keyword: 'below' -> strictly less than, no bar
steps.annotation: 'Below -18' means -18 itself is NOT cold enough -- the boundary is not included.
The temperature must be less than -18, so the small, pointed side of the symbol faces t's side... read it: 't is less than -18.'

steps.math: Check: t = -20 -> -20 < -18 is true
steps.annotation: Test a value that should work in the story. -20 is below -18, and the inequality agrees.

faded_example.stem: Students must score at least 70 points to pass the quiz. Write an inequality for s, a passing score.

steps.math: Variable: s = a passing score. Boundary: 70
steps.annotation: The letter and the limit, straight from the story.
Underline the keyword. Does 'at least 70' let a student score EXACTLY 70 and pass? What does that do to the symbol?
Write the inequality, then test it with a score of 85.

sentence_starters: The boundary number is ___ because the story says ___.
I used the symbol ___ because the value ___ equal the boundary.

skills.name: Write an inequality from a real-world situation and graph its solutions on a number line

prerequisite_skill.description: Choose the inequality that represents a real-world situation AND graph all its solutions on a number line, using the correct circle type and arrow direction.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: Lawnmowers cost at least $325. Write an inequality for x and graph its solutions.

skills.i_do_script: This skill puts two pieces together. First I write the inequality from the story (same steps as before: variable, boundary, symbol). Then I graph it. The boundary number tells me WHERE to put the circle. The symbol tells me what kind of circle (closed for ≥ or ≤, open for > or <) and which way the arrow goes (right for greater than, left for less than). Watch: 'Lawnmowers cost AT LEAST $325.' x ≥ 325. Closed circle at 325, arrow pointing RIGHT because solutions are 325 or more.

canonical_error.pattern: Student writes the correct inequality but draws the graph with the arrow in the wrong direction, or uses an open circle when the inequality includes 'or equal to.'
canonical_error.example: Student writes x ≥ 325 correctly but draws an OPEN circle at 325 with the arrow going LEFT.
canonical_error.why: Student treats writing the inequality and graphing it as two unrelated tasks instead of letting the symbol drive both decisions. They forget to re-check the symbol when moving to the graph.

redirect_script.stop: Hold up — use your inequality to check the graph.
redirect_script.prompt: Point to the symbol you wrote. Does it have a line under it? Then the circle should be filled. Does it open toward the variable? Then the arrow goes that same direction — right for >, left for <.
redirect_script.praise: Your inequality and your graph match — the symbol told you both.

vocabulary.definition: All the values that make the inequality true. An inequality has infinitely many solutions.
A graph that shows every solution to an inequality, using a circle at the boundary and an arrow showing the direction of the solution set.
The single value where the solution set starts (or stops); this is the number after the inequality symbol.

next_steps.if_pass: Move to 6AF4-S4: handle two-constraint problems with a pair of inequalities.
next_steps.if_fail: Re-teach 6AF4-S1 (matching written inequality to graph). Practice with the same constraint expressed three ways: words, inequality, graph.

skills.item_template: A one-constraint real-world situation. Part A: choose or write the inequality. Part B: graph the solutions on a number line (circle type + arrow direction). MP.

worked_example_script.text: Write: 'New lawnmowers cost at least $325.' Draw a blank number line with 325 marked near the middle.
First, the inequality. What's the variable, what's the boundary, and what's the keyword?
'At least 325' -- can the cost be exactly 325 and still be enough? So which symbol?
Write x >= 325.
Now the graph -- and here's the rule: the symbol you JUST wrote makes both graph decisions. Does >= have a bar? So what kind of circle goes at 325?
Read it variable-first: 'x is greater than or equal to 325.' Which way does the arrow go?
Draw the closed circle at 325 and the arrow pointing right. Test with 400: is $400 enough in the story? Is 400 under the arrow?
If the inequality and the graph disagree -- right symbol, wrong circle or arrow -- don't fix it. Ask the student to point at their symbol and say what it tells the circle to be and the arrow to do.

practice_problems.stem: For x >= 12, what kind of circle goes at 12 on the graph?
practice_problems.answer: Closed (filled) -- the bar means 12 is included.

practice_problems.stem: 'Fewer than 9 tickets' -- which direction will the arrow on the graph point?
practice_problems.answer: Left -- the solutions are smaller than 9.

practice_problems.stem: A ride requires riders to be at least 42 inches tall. Write an inequality for h, a rider's height, and graph the solutions on the number line.
practice_problems.answer: h >= 42; Closed circle at 42, arrow pointing right
practice_problems.notes: The full at-proficiency move: write, then let the symbol drive the graph.

practice_problems.stem: A parking garage only allows vehicles under 7 feet tall. Write an inequality for v, a vehicle's height, and graph the solutions.
practice_problems.answer: v < 7; Open circle at 7, arrow pointing left
practice_problems.notes: 'Under' is strict -- watch for a closed circle at 7.

practice_problems.stem: Lena wrote an inequality and drew a graph for this problem. Find her mistake and fix it.
shown_work: Problem: New lawnmowers cost at least $325. x = the money needed.
Lena's graph: open circle at 325, arrow pointing left
practice_problems.answer: Lena's inequality is right, but her graph doesn't match it. The bar under >= means a CLOSED circle at 325, and 'greater than' sends the arrow RIGHT. Correct graph: closed circle at 325, arrow pointing right.
practice_problems.notes: Canonical error: treating the writing and the graphing as unrelated tasks.

practice_problems.stem: Jordan must read more than 30 minutes tonight. Write an inequality for m, the minutes read, and describe its graph.
practice_problems.answer: m > 30; open circle at 30, arrow pointing right.

practice_problems.stem: A graph shows a closed circle at 55 with the arrow pointing left. Write the inequality it represents AND a real-world sentence it could describe.
practice_problems.answer: x <= 55; e.g. 'The speed limit on this road is 55 miles per hour.'
practice_problems.notes: Reversed direction: graph to inequality to story.

practice_problems.stem: How many solutions does h >= 42 have? Explain how the graph shows this.
practice_problems.answer: Infinitely many. The arrow points right and never ends -- 42, 42.5, 43, 100, and every number beyond are all solutions.
practice_problems.notes: Hits the standard's 'infinitely many solutions' demand head-on.

activities.title: Act Out the Constraint
materials: Painter's tape number line on the floor (0-60, tens labeled)
One paper circle: FILLED on one side, OPEN ring on the other
activities.instructions:
1. Read a constraint card: 'Riders must be at least 42 inches tall.'
2. The class first writes the inequality on whiteboards (h >= 42). Agree on it before anyone moves.
3. One student stands at 42 holding the circle -- filled side out, because the symbol has a bar.
4. Everyone else picks a height that gets to ride and stands on it. Ask: which way does our crowd stretch? Sweep your arm -- that's the arrow.
5. Repeat with 'under 7 feet' (scale the line) or 'more than 30 minutes.' Debrief: how did the SYMBOL tell us both the circle and the direction?

activities.title: The Symbol Says Both
materials: One printed problem card per group
activities.instructions:
1. Show Lena's work: a correct inequality next to a graph that contradicts it.
2. Ask: which half is right? How do you know?
3. Have the group fix the graph and then state the rule: the symbol makes BOTH graph decisions.
4. Each student writes a one-line checklist they'll run before turning in any graph.

content.worked_problem: Problem: lawnmowers cost at least $325. Lena wrote x >= 325 (correct), then graphed an open circle at 325 with the arrow pointing left.
content.error_step: Lena stopped consulting her own inequality when she switched to the graph -- open circle and left arrow contradict >= on both decisions.
content.why: The graph is just the inequality drawn: the bar under >= means a filled circle at 325, and 'greater than or equal' means the solutions -- and the arrow -- go right.

activities.title: Story-Symbol-Graph Line-Up
activities.instructions:
1. Spread the graph cards face up; stack the story cards.
2. Partner A flips a story, writes the inequality on a whiteboard, and reads it variable-first.
3. Partner B finds the graph that matches the WRITTEN inequality (not the story directly). Both check that story, symbol, and graph all agree.
4. Debrief question: why is it safer to go story -> inequality -> graph than story -> graph?

pairs.left: Riders must be at least 42 inches tall. (h)
pairs.right: Closed circle at 42, arrow pointing right
Open circle at 20, arrow pointing left

pairs.left: You must save more than 75 dollars. (s)
pairs.right: Open circle at 75, arrow pointing right

pairs.left: The pool holds at most 45 swimmers. (p)
pairs.right: Closed circle at 45, arrow pointing left

decoys: Closed circle at 42, arrow pointing left
Open circle at 45, arrow pointing left

strategy_links.why: Story to symbol to picture is exactly the concrete-representational-abstract chain -- CRA keeps the three forms tied together.
Thinking aloud while graphing ('the bar tells me closed... variable-first tells me right') models the self-talk that keeps symbol and graph in sync.
A correct inequality beside a contradicting graph is the ideal worked-example-plus-error pair for this skill's canonical miss.

questioning_prompts: You wrote the inequality -- now point at the symbol. What does it tell your circle to be?
Read your inequality variable-first. Which way does that send the arrow?
Pick a number under your arrow. Does it work in the STORY, not just the math?
Could you ever list all the solutions? What does the arrow say about that?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student writes the correct inequality but draws the graph with the arrow in the wrong direction, or uses an open circle when the inequality includes 'or equal to.'
misconception_redirects.say: Point to the symbol you wrote. Does it have a line under it? Then the circle should be filled. Does it open toward the variable? Then the arrow goes that same direction -- right for >, left for <.
misconception_redirects.praise: Your inequality and your graph match -- the symbol told you both.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student graphs only the boundary point (a single dot, no arrow), treating the inequality like an equation with one answer.
misconception_redirects.say: Is 325 the ONLY amount that buys the lawnmower? What about 400? 500? Every one of those is a solution -- your graph needs the arrow to show all of them.
misconception_redirects.praise: Now your graph shows infinitely many solutions -- that's what an inequality means.

quick_checks.prompt: Write and graph in 60 seconds: 'The oven must stay at most 350 degrees.' (t)
quick_checks.look_for: t <= 350 with a closed circle at 350, arrow left. A right arrow means direction flipping; an open circle means the bar is still being dropped; symbol-graph disagreement is the canonical error.

quick_checks.prompt: Your graph of h >= 42 -- name three solutions and one non-solution.
quick_checks.look_for: Three values at or above 42 (including 42 itself!) and one below. Leaving out 42 as a solution diagnoses lingering >= vs > confusion.

worked_solution.stem: New lawnmowers cost at least $325. Write an inequality for x, the money needed, and graph the solutions.
worked_solution.answer: x >= 325; closed circle at 325, arrow pointing right

steps.math: Variable: x = money needed. Boundary: 325. Keyword: 'at least'
steps.annotation: 'At least 325' means 325 or more -- exactly 325 is enough, so the boundary is included.
Greater than or equal: the bar carries the 'or equal' part of 'at least.'

steps.math: Circle: >= has a bar -> CLOSED circle at 325
steps.annotation: The symbol you wrote makes the first graph decision for you.

steps.math: Arrow: 'x is greater than or equal to 325' -> arrow RIGHT
steps.annotation: Read it variable-first; bigger numbers live to the right. Check: 400 is under the arrow, and $400 buys the mower.

faded_example.stem: A pool allows at most 45 swimmers. Write an inequality for p, the number of swimmers, and graph the solutions.
faded_example.answer: p <= 45; closed circle at 45, arrow pointing left

steps.math: Keyword: 'at most 45' -> p <= 45
steps.annotation: 45 swimmers is still allowed, so the symbol keeps its bar.
Circle decision: does <= have a bar? So what kind of circle goes at 45?
Arrow decision: read p <= 45 variable-first. Which way does the arrow point, and name one solution to check.

sentence_starters: My graph matches my inequality because the symbol ___.
The arrow points ___ because the story allows values that are ___ than ___.

skills.name: Write a pair of inequalities to represent a two-constraint real-world situation

prerequisite_skill.description: Given a real-world situation with both a lower and an upper bound, write a compound inequality (two inequalities joined by 'and') that captures both constraints.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: A playground's area must be at least 248 sq ft and no more than 328 sq ft. Write a pair of inequalities for the area a.

skills.i_do_script: Sometimes a problem has TWO constraints — a lower limit and an upper limit. I write one inequality for each, then connect them with 'and.' Watch: 'The playground area is at least 248 square feet but at most 328 square feet.' Lower: a ≥ 248. Upper: a ≤ 328. Together: a ≥ 248 AND a ≤ 328. Both inequalities have to be true at the same time — the area is squeezed between 248 and 328, including both ends because of 'at least' and 'at most.'

canonical_error.pattern: Student writes one of the two inequalities with the wrong direction, producing a pair that has no solutions (e.g., a ≥ high AND a ≤ low).
canonical_error.example: For 'between 248 and 328 sq ft,' student writes a ≥ 328 AND a ≤ 248, swapping which value is the floor and which is the ceiling.
canonical_error.why: Student is not asking 'which number is the LOW limit and which is the HIGH limit?' They mechanically pair the first number with one symbol and the second with the other without checking that the result actually describes a range.

redirect_script.stop: Pause — test your answer with a number in the middle.
redirect_script.prompt: Pick a value between the two numbers (like 300 for 248 and 328). Plug it into BOTH of your inequalities. If both come out true, you got it right. If either is false, the symbol direction is wrong on that one.
redirect_script.praise: You checked with a real value — that's how you know the pair actually fits.

vocabulary.definition: Two inequalities joined by 'and' that must both be true at the same time.
The smallest value the variable can take.
The largest value the variable can take.

next_steps.if_pass: Move to 6AF4-S5: write the inequality pair AND explain each one in context.
next_steps.if_fail: Step back to 6AF4-S2 (single constraint). Practice writing each constraint of the pair separately before combining.

skills.item_template: A real-world situation with a lower and an upper bound. Student writes or completes the pair of inequalities joined by 'and.' MC or dropdown-completion.

worked_example_script.text: Write: 'The playground area must be at least 248 square feet but no more than 328 square feet. a = the area.'
How many rules does this story put on the area? Say each one in your own words.
Which number is the FLOOR -- the smallest the area can be? Which is the CEILING?
Write just the floor rule first: 'at least 248.' What inequality is that?
Now the ceiling rule: 'no more than 328.' What inequality?
Join them with 'and': a >= 248 and a <= 328. Both rules must be true at the same time.
Test it. Pick a number between 248 and 328 -- say 300. Does 300 make BOTH inequalities true? Now try 200: which rule does it break?
If the student writes a >= 328 and a <= 248, don't say 'wrong.' Ask them to find ONE number that makes both true. When they can't, ask which number was really the floor.

practice_problems.stem: 'Between 10 and 20, inclusive' -- which number is the floor and which is the ceiling?
practice_problems.answer: Floor: 10 (the smallest allowed). Ceiling: 20 (the largest allowed).

practice_problems.stem: Write ONE inequality for 'the tank holds at least 50 gallons,' using g.
Kids ages 8 to 12, inclusive, may join the club. Write a pair of inequalities for a, a member's age.
practice_problems.answer: a >= 8 and a <= 12

practice_problems.stem: A purchase must be at least $25 but no more than $100 to earn the discount. Write the pair of inequalities for p, the purchase amount.
Kai wrote a pair of inequalities for the playground area a. Test his pair with the number 300, then fix it.
shown_work: Problem: The area must be at least 248 sq ft and no more than 328 sq ft.

skills.name: Write a pair of inequalities for a two-constraint situation and explain each in context

prerequisite_skill.description: Given a real-world situation with two constraints (often involving decimals), select or write the correct pair of inequalities and write a sentence explaining what each inequality means in the context.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: Times ranged from 23.6 to 34.8 minutes. Write a pair of inequalities for t and explain what each one means.

skills.i_do_script: This is a two-step skill. First, write the pair of inequalities (same as the last skill). Second, explain in words what each inequality means in the context of the story. Watch: 'Times ranged from 23.6 to 34.8 minutes.' Pair: t ≥ 23.6 AND t ≤ 34.8. Explanation: t ≥ 23.6 means 'the slowest possible time is the fastest student's 23.6 minutes — no one finished faster.' t ≤ 34.8 means 'the longest time is 34.8 — no one took longer.' The story decides which boundary is which.

canonical_error.pattern: Student writes the correct pair of inequalities but the explanation flips which boundary corresponds to which real-world condition (fastest vs. slowest, lowest vs. highest).
canonical_error.example: Student says 't ≤ 34.8 means the slowest student' when 34.8 is actually the slowest time, so ≤ 34.8 means everyone else was at or below the slowest — they have the role right but say it backwards.
canonical_error.why: Student is matching numbers to inequality symbols mechanically without re-reading the story to see which extreme each number represents in the situation.

redirect_script.stop: Wait — read your explanation against the story.
redirect_script.prompt: Look at each number. Which one came from the FASTEST student (or LOWEST measurement)? Which came from the SLOWEST (or HIGHEST)? Re-write your explanation so it names the role each number plays in the story.
redirect_script.praise: You connected each inequality back to the actual story — that's the proof you understand it.

vocabulary.definition: Two inequalities joined by 'and' that both must be true at the same time.
A rule from the situation that limits which values are allowed.
Every value that makes both inequalities true — the range between the two bounds.

worked_example_script.text: Write: 'A group of students ran a scavenger hunt. The first student finished in 23.6 minutes. The last student finished in 34.8 minutes. t = any student's time.'
Two numbers in this story. What ROLE does each one play -- who produced 23.6, and who produced 34.8?
If the FASTEST student took 23.6 minutes, could anyone have a time under 23.6? So what must be true of every time t?
If the SLOWEST student took 34.8, what's the other rule for t?
Write the pair: t >= 23.6 and t <= 34.8.
Now the explaining part. Say what t >= 23.6 means using the story's words -- start with 'No one finished faster than...'
If the explanation attaches a boundary to the wrong person -- '34.8 was the fastest' -- send them back to the story: 'Which student created that number? Point to the sentence.'
The math and the sentence must tell the same story: every boundary number belongs to a specific person or event in the problem, and your explanation has to name it.

skills.name: Match a written inequality with a whole-number boundary to its number-line graph

prerequisite_skill.description: Before tackling rational-number boundaries, students need to match inequalities to number-line graphs when the boundary is a whole number, so they can isolate the open-vs-closed-circle and arrow-direction decisions from the harder task of locating a fraction or decimal on the line.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: Which number line represents x ≤ 5? (closed circle at 5, arrow pointing left)

skills.i_do_script: A graph can't be judged by its overall shape -- it's judged by which numbers it covers. So test a few numbers in x <= 5 first and let the pass/fail list pick the picture. When I match an inequality to a number line, I make TWO decisions. First, the circle: if the symbol has a bar under it (≤ or ≥), I use a CLOSED circle because the boundary is included. If it has no bar (< or >), I use an OPEN circle because the boundary is NOT included. Second, the arrow: I read the inequality with the variable FIRST. 'x < 5' means 'x is less than 5,' so the arrow points LEFT toward smaller numbers. 'x > 5' means 'x is greater than 5,' so the arrow points RIGHT toward bigger numbers. Watch: x ≤ 5. The bar means CLOSED circle at 5. 'x is less than or equal to 5' means arrow points LEFT. Closed circle at 5, arrow left.

canonical_error.pattern: Student picks the right boundary point but uses the wrong circle type or wrong arrow direction because they aren't separating the two decisions — they grab a graph that 'looks about right' instead of checking circle AND direction independently.
canonical_error.example: For x ≥ 4, student picks an OPEN circle at 4 with the arrow pointing right, ignoring that the bar under ≥ means the boundary is included.
canonical_error.why: Even with a friendly whole-number boundary, the student conflates the two graph features into one fuzzy 'shape' judgment. Stripping the boundary down to a whole number makes it obvious that the only thing left to get right is circle type and direction — the exact decisions S1 hammers, but with the rational-number distraction removed.

worked_example_script.text: Before looking at any sketch, test three numbers in x <= 5. Does 3 pass? (Yes.) Does 7 pass? (No.) Does 5 itself pass? (Yes -- 5 is 'less than OR EQUAL to' 5.)
So the true graph must cover 3, skip 7, and include 5 itself. Hold those three verdicts up against the two sketches -- only one can survive.
Write x <= 5 on the board. Sketch two number lines: one with a closed circle at 5 and the arrow pointing left, one with an open circle at 5 and the arrow pointing right.
Look at the symbol in x <= 5. What do you notice about it besides the 'less than' part?
That bar underneath means 'or equal to.' So is 5 itself allowed to be a solution?
If 5 IS a solution, should the circle at 5 be filled in or hollow?
Now the arrow. Read the inequality with the variable first: 'x is less than or equal to 5.' Are the solutions bigger or smaller than 5? Which way do smaller numbers live on a number line?
Trace the correct graph: closed circle at 5, arrow pointing left. Cross out the other one.
If the student picks a graph because it 'looks right,' back up and make them answer the two questions separately: circle first (is there a bar?), then arrow (variable-first, which direction?).
Two decisions, every single time: the bar under the symbol decides the circle, and reading it variable-first decides the arrow.

practice_problems.stem: Does the symbol >= include the boundary number, or leave it out?
practice_problems.answer: It includes it -- the bar under the symbol means 'or equal to.'

practice_problems.stem: For x < 9, do the solutions live to the left or the right of 9 on a number line?
practice_problems.answer: To the left -- the solutions are all smaller than 9.

practice_problems.stem: Graph the solutions of x >= 4 on the number line.
practice_problems.answer: Closed circle at 4, arrow pointing right
practice_problems.notes: Both decisions at once: bar means closed, greater-than means arrow right.

practice_problems.stem: Which number line represents t < 7: an open circle at 7 with the arrow left, or a closed circle at 7 with the arrow left?
practice_problems.answer: Open circle at 7, arrow left -- 7 is not a solution because < has no bar under it.

practice_problems.stem: Marcus graphed the inequality n >= 6. Find his mistake and fix it.
shown_work: Marcus's graph: open circle at 6, arrow pointing right
practice_problems.answer: The arrow direction is right, but the circle must be CLOSED. The bar under >= means 6 itself is a solution, so the circle at 6 is filled in.
practice_problems.notes: Bait for the canonical error: getting the boundary and direction right but missing the open-vs-closed decision.

practice_problems.stem: Graph the solutions of m <= 2 on the number line.
practice_problems.answer: Closed circle at 2, arrow pointing left
practice_problems.notes: Watch for an open circle -- the bar under <= means 2 is included.

practice_problems.stem: Is 5 a solution of x < 5? Explain how the graph shows your answer.
practice_problems.answer: No. The graph has an OPEN circle at 5, which means 5 itself is not included -- the solutions are every number below 5.

practice_problems.stem: A number line shows a closed circle at 10 with the arrow pointing left. Write the inequality it represents.
practice_problems.notes: Reversed direction: graph to symbols instead of symbols to graph.

activities.title: Open or Closed?
materials: Two header cards: OPEN circle, CLOSED circle
activities.instructions:
1. Lay the two header cards on the desk: OPEN circle and CLOSED circle.
2. Partners take turns drawing an inequality card, reading it aloud, and placing it under the right header.
3. The rule to say out loud every time: 'Bar under the symbol means closed. No bar means open.'
4. After sorting, each partner picks one card and says which way its arrow would point and why.
5. Debrief question: which two symbols always mean a closed circle?

activities.title: Human Number Line
materials: Painter's tape line on the floor labeled 0-10
One hula hoop or paper circle (one side marked OPEN, other side FILLED)
activities.instructions:
1. Make a number line on the floor with tape, labeled 0 through 10.
2. Show an inequality card, like x >= 4. One student is the 'boundary': they stand at 4 holding the circle -- FILLED side out if the symbol has a bar, OPEN side out if not.
3. Every other student picks any number that makes the inequality true and stands on it. Students who can't find a spot stand off the line.
4. Ask the class: which direction does the crowd stretch? That's the arrow.
5. Repeat with x < 7 and t > 2. Debrief question: could we ever run out of places to stand? (No -- infinitely many solutions; the line just ends before the solutions do.)

activities.title: Fix Marcus's Graph
materials: One printed problem card per group
activities.instructions:
1. Show the group Marcus's graph of n >= 6 and let them talk before you do.
2. Ask: what did Marcus get RIGHT? (Boundary at 6, arrow pointing right.)
3. Ask: what one thing is wrong, and which part of the symbol did he ignore?
4. Each student writes Marcus a one-sentence tip about the bar under the symbol.

content.worked_problem: Inequality: n >= 6. Marcus's graph: open circle at 6, arrow pointing right.
content.error_step: Marcus drew an open circle at 6, treating >= exactly like >.
content.why: The bar under >= means 'or equal to' -- 6 itself is a solution, so the circle must be filled in. Only < and > (no bar) get open circles.

strategy_links.why: Fast choral rounds -- 'bar or no bar? open or closed?' -- make the circle decision automatic.
Whiteboard Pass shows every student's circle-and-arrow sketch at once, so one fuzzy 'looks right' choice can't hide.
Analyzing a graph with the right boundary but wrong circle isolates exactly the decision this skill's canonical error skips.

questioning_prompts: Before you look at any graph: does the symbol have a bar under it? What does that tell you?
Read the inequality with the variable FIRST. Is x bigger or smaller than the boundary?
You picked this graph -- name the two things about it that match the inequality.
Pick a number the arrow covers. Does it actually make the inequality true?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student picks the right boundary point but the wrong circle type or arrow direction -- they grab a graph that 'looks about right' instead of checking circle AND direction separately.
misconception_redirects.say: Walk me through what you did. Show each step out loud -- circle decision first, then arrow decision.
misconception_redirects.praise: You worked through it carefully -- that's exactly the right move.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student reads x < 7 right-to-left and sends the arrow to the right, toward the bigger numbers.
misconception_redirects.say: Put your finger on the variable and read from there: 'x is less than 7.' If x is SMALLER than 7, which side of 7 do the solutions live on?
misconception_redirects.praise: You read it variable-first and the arrow followed -- that's the habit.

quick_checks.prompt: Thumbs up or down: the graph of x >= 3 has an open circle.
quick_checks.look_for: An instant thumbs-down. Hesitation or a thumbs-up means the bar-means-closed rule isn't set -- reteach the circle decision before doing any more matching.

quick_checks.prompt: Sketch the graph of n < 10 in the air: point to where the circle goes, then sweep the arrow.
quick_checks.look_for: Circle gesture at 10 and a sweep to the left. A sweep right diagnoses symbol reversal; a 'filled' fist at 10 diagnoses open/closed confusion.

steps.annotation: Greater means the solutions are bigger than 4, and bigger numbers live to the RIGHT on a number line.

progression.narrative: This standard asks students to write an inequality like x > c or x <= c from a real-world constraint, explain that it has infinitely many solutions, and show those solutions on a number line. The on-grade work runs from matching a written inequality to its graph, through writing an inequality from a story, to the full move of writing and graphing in one motion, where the symbol decides both the circle type and the arrow direction. Students who struggle here usually cannot read comparison symbols reliably, cannot compare two decimals, or cannot locate a fraction or decimal on a number line, all skills from well below grade six. Intervention should start with whole number comparison and simple number line plotting, rebuild the grade five skills of comparing decimals and plotting fractions and decimals, and only then return to inequalities with a variable.

steps.rationale: Isolate the two graph decisions -- circle type and arrow direction -- with whole-number boundaries, before rational numbers add a locating step. Every later graph rests on these two decisions.
Extend matching to rational boundaries (fractions, decimals, negatives). The standard says c is any rational number, so students must locate the boundary as well as read the symbol.
The standard's first demand: write an inequality from a real-world constraint. Variable, boundary, keyword -- and the keyword decides whether the boundary itself is allowed.
The standard's full on-grade demand: write the inequality AND represent its infinitely many solutions on a number line, with the symbol driving both graph decisions.
Extension: two constraints at once. Students write a pair of inequalities with a floor and a ceiling, and test a middle value to prove the pair actually describes a range.
The deepest demand: connect each inequality of a pair back to the situation in words. Explaining which boundary belongs to which part of the story shows the symbols carry meaning.

diagnostic_flow.description: Start with S3, writing an inequality from a real-world constraint and graphing its solutions, the At proficiency core. If they pass, move up to S4 and S5, the two constraint pair problems. If they fail, drop below grade level: B1 checks decimal comparison to the thousandths and B2 checks plotting fractions and decimals on a number line, the two grade 5 skills that boundary work leans on. If those wobble, the foundations F1 (whole number comparison symbols), F2 (fractions on a number line), and F3 (decimal comparison to hundredths) locate the gap in grades 3 and 4. S6, S1, and S2 remain available to probe the standard's own matching and writing groundwork.
